html:
The Little Ice Age was a long period of cooler climate, strongest around the North Atlantic, conventionally placed between about 1300 or 1500 and 1850. The chart marks its harshest stretch, roughly 1643 to 1715, when cold, wet summers ruined harvests in Europe and Asia alike.

It was not a true ice age: average temperatures fell by perhaps a degree or less, unevenly across places and decades. But that was enough to shorten growing seasons and bring frosts at the wrong time. Alpine glaciers advanced and swallowed farms, and the Thames froze hard enough for frost fairs on the ice.

Possible causes, still debated:

  • Low solar activity, including the Maunder Minimum (about 1645 to 1715), when sunspots almost vanished.
  • Large volcanic eruptions that put dust into the upper air.
  • Shifts in ocean circulation.

The 1600s are sometimes called the General Crisis: wars, revolts and famine across the world, including the Thirty Years' War and the fall of the Ming in China. Many historians link these to the cold. The 1690s were especially bad; a famine in 1696 to 1697 killed perhaps a quarter to a third of the people of Finland.

Fernand Braudel noticed that populations in Europe, China and India rose and fell at about the same times, and suggested that climate might be the shared cause. Later on, cold years shaped events too: the hunger that helped spark the French Revolution followed a bad harvest in 1788.
